lessons.title: The Buddha and the Four Noble Truths
lessons.overall_verdict: FAIL — HIGH severity error on Four Sights citation

issues.category: Wrong canonical citation — Jataka vs Pali suttas
issues.quoted_text: These are recorded in Jataka 075 in the Pali Canon.
issues.problem: The lesson attributes the Four Sights narrative to 'Jataka 075 in the Pali Canon' and applies it directly to Siddhartha Gautama. This is significantly misleading on two levels. First, the Four Sights as a discrete four-encounter narrative belongs in early Pali Canon only in the Mahapadana Sutta (DN 14), where it describes the previous Buddha Vipassi — not Siddhartha. The application of the Four Sights narrative to Siddhartha himself appears only in later, post-canonical texts (Nidanakatha, Buddhavamsa, Lalitavistara). Second, Jataka 075 is part of the Jataka commentary (Jatakatthavananna), an extensive prose commentary compiled c. 5th century CE by Buddhaghosa — it is NOT a primary sutta of the Sutta Pitaka. The Jataka verses are canonical; the narrative stories are commentarial. Citing 'Jataka 075 in the Pali Canon' as the authoritative canonical source for Siddhartha's Four Sights is incorrect. The AQA specification is primarily Theravada-oriented; students who cite this in an exam would be stating something that leading scholarship considers post-canonical tradition, not early Pali Canon.
issues.correction: Remove 'These are recorded in Jataka 075 in the Pali Canon.' The Four Sights for Siddhartha are a biographical tradition attested in later texts (Nidanakatha, Lalitavistara). In the early Pali Canon (DN 14, Mahapadana Sutta), the Four Sights are attributed to Buddha Vipassi. Students should be told: 'The Four Sights are a key biographical story in Buddhist tradition. The early Pali Canon describes similar encounters in the life of a previous Buddha, Vipassi (DN 14); the full narrative as applied to Siddhartha develops in later Buddhist literature.'

issues.category: Buddha life dates — acceptable but incomplete
issues.quoted_text: traditionally dated around the 5th century BCE in Lumbini
issues.problem: The lesson uses 'around the 5th century BCE' which is acceptably vague. The audit brief asks to verify the c. 563–483 BCE traditional dates vs c. 480–400 BCE modern scholarly range. The lesson avoids committing to specific dates, which is pedagogically appropriate given scholarly uncertainty. No error, but students should know the traditional dates are 'c. 563–483 BCE' for exam answers.
issues.correction: Consider adding the traditional dates (c. 563–483 BCE) explicitly, noting modern scholarship suggests possibly c. 480–400 BCE.

issues.quoted_text: Underlying tanha are the Three Poisons — the Three Poisons of ignorance (moha), greed (lobha) and hatred (dosa).
issues.problem: Minor duplication in phrasing ('the Three Poisons — the Three Poisons of...') but the content is correct. Moha/lobha/dosa are the standard Pali terms. Some traditions list 'dosa' as aversion/hatred/ill-will rather than specifically 'hatred'. This is an acceptable translation variation.
issues.correction: Fix the repeated 'the Three Poisons' phrasing. Content is doctrinally accurate.

lessons.title: The Eightfold Path and Buddhist Ethics
lessons.overall_verdict: FAIL — HIGH severity error on Dhammapada citation

issues.category: Wrong Dhammapada verse cited for Threefold Way
issues.quoted_text: The Dhammapada (verses 190–191) refers to the path as the Threefold Way, grouping the eight factors into three categories: sila (ethics), samadhi (meditation) and panna (wisdom).
issues.problem: Dhammapada verses 190–191 do NOT describe or name the Threefold Way (sila/samadhi/panna). These verses (from Chapter 14, Buddhavagga) are about taking refuge in the Three Jewels and seeing the Four Noble Truths: 'He who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Teaching and his Order, penetrates with transcendental wisdom the Four Noble Truths — suffering, the cause of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the Noble Eightfold Path.' The Threefold Way grouping (sila/samadhi/panna) of the Eightfold Path is a standard doctrinal categorisation that appears throughout the canon but is especially associated with Chapter 20 of the Dhammapada (Magga Vagga), particularly verses 273 onwards, which praise the Eightfold Path. Verse 273 states: 'Of all paths the Eightfold Path is the best.' There is no Dhammapada reference that specifically names 'the Threefold Way' by grouping the eight factors. The lesson has either confused the verse numbers or fabricated a citation. This is a HIGH severity factual error that would mislead students in exams.
issues.correction: Remove the specific Dhammapada 190–191 citation for the Threefold Way. State simply: 'The Noble Eightfold Path is traditionally grouped into three dimensions: ethics (sila), meditation (samadhi) and wisdom (panna). The Dhammapada Chapter 20 (Magga Vagga, v.273) affirms the Eightfold Path as the supreme path.' Do not attribute the Threefold grouping to Dhp 190–191.

issues.category: Key Fact repeats the wrong citation
issues.location: Key Fact box immediately after The Eightfold Path section
issues.quoted_text: The Dhammapada 190–191 names this Threefold structure as the path to nibbana.
issues.problem: This Key Fact box repeats the incorrect citation from the main text. It will be seen and memorised by students. Dhp 190–191 names the Three Refuges and the Four Noble Truths, not the Threefold Way.
issues.correction: Remove the erroneous Key Fact citation. Correct to reflect what Dhp 190–191 actually says, or reference the correct chapter for the Eightfold Path (Dhp Chapter 20).

lessons.title: The Dhamma and the Three Marks of Existence

issues.quoted_text: The Buddha did not simply deny that experience exists — he denied that there is a fixed, permanent, independent 'self' standing behind our experiences.
issues.problem: The explanation is sound and accurately reflects the scholarly consensus. The 'Misconception' box correctly addresses the common misreading. No error — this is a LOW note that the lesson handles this nuance well and better than most GCSE resources.

issues.quoted_text: The Three Marks of Existence are anicca (impermanence), anatta (no fixed self) and dukkha (unsatisfactoriness/suffering).
issues.problem: The standard canonical ordering in the Pali tradition is typically anicca, dukkha, anatta (as in AN 3.136 and numerous suttas). The lesson presents anicca, anatta, dukkha. This reordering is common in pedagogical contexts but is not the canonical sequence. For AQA GCSE purposes this is unlikely to be examined as an ordering issue, but it diverges from the Pali Canon sequence.
issues.correction: Minor: consider reordering to anicca, dukkha, anatta to match the canonical sequence. Not an error that would mislead students on exam answers.

lessons.title: The Human Personality and Human Destiny

issues.location: Section: Mahayana Buddhism: Sunyata and Buddha-Nature
issues.quoted_text: Buddha-nature is not a 'self' but rather a luminous quality of awareness that can be uncovered when ignorance and craving are removed.
issues.problem: This is a defensible summary but simplifies a complex area. The tathagatagarbha teaching has been interpreted variously across Mahayana schools — some (Yogacara) treat it as closely related to sunyata, others (Tathāgatagarbha sutras) describe it in more substantialist terms that critics argue border on a hidden 'self'. The lesson's framing ('not a self') represents the dominant scholarly/Madhyamaka interpretation but glosses over an internal Mahayana debate. For GCSE purposes this is an acceptable simplification.
issues.correction: Acceptable simplification for GCSE. No change required.

lessons.title: Places of Worship and Puja

issues.quoted_text: the earth-touching gesture (bhumisparshamudra) recalls the moment of Enlightenment
issues.problem: The correct Sanskrit transliteration is 'bhumisparsha mudra' (two words) or 'bhūmisparśa mudrā'. The compound 'bhumisparshamudra' as one word is non-standard. Minor transliteration issue, not a factual error.

issues.quoted_text: Puja is the Pali/Sanskrit word for devotional ritual.
issues.problem: 'Puja' is primarily a Sanskrit word adopted into Pali as 'puja'. Calling it 'Pali/Sanskrit' is acceptable shorthand but technically the word has Sanskrit origins. No material error for GCSE purposes.

lessons.title: Meditation: Samatha, Vipassana and Visualisation

issues.category: Samatha described as the prerequisite for vipassana — contested
issues.quoted_text: a calm mind is necessary before deeper insight meditation can bear fruit
issues.problem: The lesson presents samatha as a required precondition for vipassana, which reflects one Theravada position (the 'tranquillity vehicle' approach) but is contested within Theravada itself. The 'dry insight' (sukkhavipassaka) tradition holds that samatha is not a prerequisite — insight can arise through direct observation without prior jhana attainment. This is a significant internal Theravada debate. The lesson's framing may mislead students into thinking samatha is universally required before vipassana.
issues.correction: Add a qualifier: 'Many teachers hold that samatha provides a useful foundation for vipassana, though some Theravada traditions (the dry-insight approach) teach that insight can arise without prior samatha cultivation.' This better reflects the range of canonical and traditional positions.

issues.location: Section: Zazen: meditation in Zen Buddhism
issues.quoted_text: 'What is the sound of one hand clapping?' — designed to break through conceptual thinking and reveal direct insight (satori)
issues.problem: This is a correct and widely recognised example. The lesson's description of zazen and koan practice is accurate. Satori as 'direct insight' is acceptable shorthand for kensho/satori. No factual error.

lessons.title: Death, Funeral Rites and Festivals

issues.location: Section: Tibetan Buddhist death practices and the Bardo
issues.quoted_text: The Bardo Thodol (known in the West as the 'Tibetan Book of the Dead') is read aloud to or near the dying and newly dead person to guide their consciousness through the bardo
issues.problem: The description is broadly correct. However, the lesson simplifies the Bardo Thodol as primarily a text 'read aloud.' The full Tibetan title is 'Bardo Thodol' meaning 'Liberation Through Hearing in the Intermediate State' — the emphasis is specifically on hearing, which the lesson omits. The text is read by a lama to help the consciousness of the dying/dead recognise the clear light of awareness. The lesson accurately describes the bardo as an intermediate state and the 49-day process is correctly implied. No material factual error, but the 'liberation through hearing' mechanism — central to the text's Tibetan title — is not mentioned.
issues.correction: Consider adding: 'The text is called the Bardo Thodol — meaning Liberation Through Hearing — because reading it aloud to the dying or newly dead is understood to trigger liberation through the act of hearing.' This explains the title and mechanism more accurately.

issues.quoted_text: the forty-ninth day (particularly significant as it marks the end of the bardic or transitional state in some traditions)
issues.problem: The word 'bardic' appears to be a typo or auto-correct error for 'bardo' (the Tibetan term). The 49-day transitional period is a standard Buddhist belief across several traditions, not limited to Tibetan Buddhism. The term 'bardo' is Tibetan — Japanese Buddhism uses different terminology for the intermediate state (chūu or chūin). The cross-tradition application of 'bardo' here is a minor Theravada/Mahayana terminological confusion.
issues.correction: Replace 'bardic or transitional state' with 'intermediate state (known in Tibetan Buddhism as the bardo)'. Clarify that the 49-day period is observed in Japanese Buddhist traditions independently of the Tibetan bardo concept.

issues.quoted_text: One of his last teachings, as recorded in the Tipitaka, urged his followers: 'All conditioned things are impermanent. Strive for your liberation with diligence.'
issues.problem: This is a paraphrase of the last words in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta (DN 16). The canonical Pali is 'Vayadhamma sankhara, appamadena sampadetha' — typically translated as 'All conditioned things are impermanent. Strive on with diligence' (Thanissaro Bhikkhu) or 'All compounded things are subject to vanish. Strive with earnestness.' The lesson's version ('Strive for your liberation with diligence') adds 'for your liberation' which is not in the original Pali. This is an over-interpreted paraphrase. Minor issue — the meaning is consistent but the added phrase makes it more individualistic than the canonical text.
issues.correction: Use a standard translation: 'All conditioned things are impermanent — strive on with diligence.' Remove 'for your liberation' as this is not in the original.

lessons.title: Ethics in Daily Life: Precepts and Perfections

issues.location: Section: The Five Moral Precepts in Daily Life
issues.quoted_text: In Tibetan and Japanese Buddhist traditions, meat-eating has historically been more acceptable; Mahayana texts are generally stronger in recommending a plant-based diet.
issues.problem: This creates an apparent contradiction within the same sentence. The lesson says Tibetan/Japanese allow meat, then says Mahayana texts are stronger on plant-based diet — but Tibetan and Japanese Buddhism are Mahayana traditions. The statement is broadly accurate (some Mahayana sutras like the Lankavatara Sutra do discourage meat; Tibetan climate made vegetarianism impractical historically; Japanese Zen traditions have complex histories). However, the phrasing is potentially confusing for students.
issues.correction: Clarify: 'In some Mahayana traditions such as Tibetan and Japanese Buddhism, meat-eating has historically been more acceptable due to climate and local custom, despite certain Mahayana scriptures (such as the Lankavatara Sutra) recommending a plant-based diet. There is thus variation within Mahayana on this point.'

issues.category: Six Perfections — Pali vs Sanskrit terminology
issues.problem: The Six Perfections are a Mahayana Sanskrit concept (paramitas). Using Pali terms (dana, khanti, viriya) alongside Sanskrit (prajna) is inconsistent. The Sanskrit paramitas are: dana, sila, ksanti, virya, dhyana, prajna. Using mixed Pali/Sanskrit terminology for a Mahayana teaching is a minor terminological inconsistency.
issues.correction: Use consistent Sanskrit terminology throughout for the Six Perfections, as this is a Mahayana teaching: dana (generosity), sila (morality), ksanti (patience), virya (energy), dhyana (meditation), prajna (wisdom). Or use Pali throughout with a note that they are Pali approximations of the Sanskrit paramitas.

top_3_worst_lessons.title: The Buddha and the Four Noble Truths
top_3_worst_lessons.reason: Cites 'Jataka 075 in the Pali Canon' as the canonical source for Siddhartha's Four Sights. This is doubly wrong: (a) the Four Sights narrative in early Pali Canon (DN 14, Mahapadana Sutta) belongs to the previous Buddha Vipassi, not Siddhartha; (b) Jataka 075 is part of the Jatakatthavananna commentary (c. 5th century CE), not a primary Sutta Pitaka text. A student citing this in an exam would be presenting a post-canonical biographical tradition as a canonical primary source.

top_3_worst_lessons.title: The Eightfold Path and Buddhist Ethics
top_3_worst_lessons.reason: Dhammapada verses 190–191 are cited as naming the Threefold Way (sila/samadhi/panna). These verses do not do this — they describe the Three Refuges and the Four Noble Truths. The error appears twice (main text + Key Fact box). Students who memorise this citation for an exam will be wrong about a core scriptural reference in the most foundational lesson on the Eightfold Path.

top_3_worst_lessons.title: Death, Funeral Rites and Festivals
top_3_worst_lessons.reason: Three compounding issues: 'bardic' typo for 'bardo' (potentially confusing); the Bardo Thodol's central mechanism ('liberation through hearing') not explained despite being in the title; and the Buddha's last words are paraphrased with 'for your liberation' added — a phrase not present in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta. No single issue is critical but the cluster lowers confidence in this lesson's scriptural accuracy.

general_observations: The four Beliefs lessons show more scriptural citation risk than the four Practices lessons. The two HIGH severity errors are both in Beliefs lessons and both involve specific textual citations that are wrong.
The Practices lessons (L1–L4) are generally well-researched. Issues are terminological or nuance-level rather than factual errors about canonical content.
Theravada vs Mahayana distinctions are handled consistently well across all eight lessons — the lessons avoid conflating traditions and correctly flag when a concept is tradition-specific.
The Three Marks of Existence, Five Aggregates, Four Noble Truths, Five Precepts, and bodhisattva/arhat contrast are all accurately presented.

The main vulnerability is specific Dhammapada/Jataka citations — both high-severity errors involve a citation being wrong or misapplied. These should be audited in any RE lesson that names a specific sutta or verse number.
